factChecks.claimText: 2,000 new permanent jobs for Allen County residents
factChecks.findingHeadline: CBRE models 1,676 Allen County jobs—not 2,000 permanent jobs for Allen County residents—and even that is not a net-jobs total
factChecks.shortFinding: CBRE says 947 of the 1,676 are direct jobs at the proposed casino. The rest are estimates of additional jobs supported elsewhere. It does not subtract jobs lost when residents shift money and workers away from local restaurants, hotels, retailers, entertainment, and other businesses. So neither 2,000 nor 1,676 is a count of net new local jobs.
factChecks.detailedExplanation:
Yes for Allen promotes ‘over 2,000 new permanent jobs’ for Allen County residents. The underlying CBRE table instead lists 1,676 Allen County jobs: 947 direct jobs, 309 indirect jobs, and 420 induced jobs. Its 2,001 total is statewide, not an Allen County count.

The 729 indirect and induced jobs are RIMS II multiplier estimates, not casino payroll positions. BEA explains that RIMS II employment includes full- and part-time jobs and estimates the later rounds of activity from a change in final demand. Neither figure establishes where workers would live.

The larger problem is that the published CBRE analysis shows an adjustment for revenue displaced from existing Indiana casinos, but does not show a corresponding deduction for consumer spending shifted from Allen County restaurants, entertainment, retail, hotels, or other local businesses. Without that economy-wide substitution adjustment, the multiplier total is a gross impact—not a demonstrated net gain in local jobs.
keyFacts: Allen County: 947 direct jobs, plus 309 indirect and 420 induced RIMS II estimates, totaling 1,676.
Statewide: 1,024 direct jobs plus 977 indirect and induced jobs, totaling 2,001—not 2,001 Allen County jobs.
CBRE shows casino-to-casino displacement but not a published deduction for non-casino local-business substitution.

factChecks.claimText: A casino would keep Northeast Indiana’s gambling dollars local
factChecks.findingHeadline: Most projected casino revenue would come from the regional market — not from out-of-state money
factChecks.shortFinding: Casino revenue is not money returned to residents; it is the money gamblers lose after winnings are paid. Spectrum expects only a small share of revenue from other states, meaning most projected revenue would come from gamblers in the casino’s core regional market. Calling those losses ‘dollars kept local’ confuses casino income with community wealth.
factChecks.detailedExplanation:
Yes for Allen says a casino would ‘bring that revenue back and put it to work here for Allen County residents.’

But a casino can generate that revenue only by retaining gamblers’ money after paying winnings. When the gamblers are local residents, the casino’s revenue is a direct loss to local households—not money returned to them or newly created for the community.

Spectrum expects only a small percentage of the casino’s revenue to come from other states. Most would therefore come from its core regional market. Taxes, employee wages, and local purchases may recirculate a portion, but that does not make the casino’s entire revenue a local benefit—especially when gambling displaces spending at other local businesses.
keyFacts: Adjusted gross receipts are wagers retained by the casino after winnings and limited deductions.
Spectrum expects only a small percentage of revenue from out-of-state gamblers.
Local gambling losses can replace household spending at existing restaurants, entertainment venues, and other businesses.

factChecks.claimText: A tribal casino would require no state or local approval
factChecks.findingHeadline: The ordinary off-reservation Class III casino path requires state participation
factChecks.shortFinding: Federal law governs tribal gaming, but it does not eliminate state and local participation. The ordinary off-reservation route requires the Governor’s concurrence and consultation with state and local officials; Class III casino gaming also requires a Tribal-State compact.
factChecks.detailedExplanation: Yes for Allen states: ‘A tribal casino would be governed by federal law and would not require approval from state or local officials.’ A tribe cannot simply build a casino on ordinary land in Allen County. Gaming must occur on eligible Indian lands, and IGRA generally prohibits gaming on land taken into trust after October 17, 1988 unless a statutory exception applies. Under the two-part Secretarial Determination route, Interior must consult appropriate state and local officials, determine that gaming would not harm the surrounding community, and obtain the Governor’s affirmative concurrence. Full-scale Class III casino gaming additionally requires a Tribal-State compact approved by the U.S. Department of the Interior. Local officials do not possess a universal veto under every possible IGRA exception, but Yes for Allen’s categorical statement that no state or local approval is required is false.
keyFacts: The Fort Wayne parcel entered trust in 2024, so Section 2719 gaming-land rules are relevant.
The two-part Secretarial Determination route requires affirmative Governor concurrence.
Appropriate state and local officials are consulted on the two-part route.
Class III gaming ordinarily requires a valid Tribal-State compact approved by Interior.

factChecks.claimText: Casinos provide net decreases to taxpayer liabilities
factChecks.findingHeadline: No cited evidence shows that a Steuben casino would reduce residents’ tax liabilities
factChecks.shortFinding: No cited evidence shows that a Steuben casino would reduce taxpayer liabilities. Casino payments go to government accounts, not automatically back to residents, and no law requires a tax cut. Without subtracting added public costs from projected receipts, the campaign cannot claim a net taxpayer benefit.
factChecks.detailedExplanation:
Steuben’s promotional site claims casinos ‘provide net decreases to taxpayer liabilities.’

HEA 1038 creates government revenue streams; it does not send casino money to taxpayers or require local officials to lower anyone’s tax bill. A limited budgeting option for a one-year levy reduction is not evidence that household taxes would actually fall, and it does not lower the unit’s maximum levy.

A net-liability claim requires a complete accounting of revenue, added infrastructure and public-service costs, gambling-related costs, and local budget decisions. Steuben’s own page says its third-party impact study is still in progress. It therefore has no completed analysis establishing a net decrease for taxpayers.
keyFacts: HEA 1038 requires no reduction in residents’ tax bills.
Government receipts are not a net benefit until added public costs are subtracted.
Steuben says its own third-party impact study is still in progress.

factChecks.claimText: The new Steuben casino would be legally required to fund local nonprofits through a Local Development Agreement
factChecks.findingHeadline: Indiana law does not require a Steuben casino to fund local nonprofits through an LDA
factChecks.shortFinding: HEA 1038 mandates a 3.5% supplemental wagering tax distributed to the host municipality, host county, and regional development authority. It does not mandate a Local Development Agreement or grants to nonprofits.
factChecks.detailedExplanation: The Steuben site presents nonprofit grants through Local Development Agreements as a required destination for funds from the proposed casino. Existing Indiana casinos may have contractual local agreements, but the Northeast Indiana casino statute does not create that requirement. A future applicant could propose voluntary local commitments, but that is different from a legal mandate and cannot be promised before applications are filed and a license is awarded.
keyFacts: The supplemental tax is 3.5% of adjusted gross receipts, not a mandated share of profits.
The statutory recipients are the host municipality, host county, and Northeast Indiana regional development authority.
No applicant or project has yet been selected, so any additional local agreement remains unestablished.

factChecks.claimText: A Detroit property-value study proves casinos help surrounding businesses instead of displacing them
factChecks.findingHeadline: Commercial-property sales do not measure the substitution effect on local businesses
factChecks.shortFinding: The cited Detroit study tracked commercial-property sale prices—not the customer spending, revenue, profits, jobs, or closures of nearby businesses. It therefore cannot refute whether casino spending displaces money from those businesses.
factChecks.detailedExplanation:
Steuben’s promotional site cites a Detroit study of commercial-property values around casinos to dispute the substitution effect. But a building’s sale price is not a measure of how nearby restaurants, entertainment venues, hotels, or retailers perform after casino spending enters the market.

The Detroit study did not track whether those businesses gained or lost customers, revenue, profits, jobs, or whether any closed. It did not measure the share of casino spending diverted from existing local businesses.

Research that examines industry-level sales addresses that separate operating question and finds substitution between casinos and entertainment and amusement businesses. A property-sales result cannot rebut evidence about business revenue displacement.
keyFacts: Commercial-property sale prices are not business revenue, customer spending, profit, employment, or closure data.
The Detroit study did not measure whether casino spending displaced spending from nearby businesses.
Separate sales research found casinos substitute for entertainment and amusement spending.
